ch27.d.sw: Charge from the battery, or discharge through the resistor with the battery out. Switching while running takes effect at that instant
ch27.goal.exp: Charging and discharging an RC circuit: charge and current change exponentially
ch27.goal.tau: One time constant $\tau = RC$ sets how fast
ch27.obs.tau: At $t = \tau$ the charge has covered 63 % of the way to its final value and the current has dropped to 37 %
ch27.obs.tangent: The tangent at the switching instant (dashed) reaches the final value at $t = \tau$
ch27.obs.i: The current starts at its maximum $\mathcal{E}/R$ and falls to 0: as the capacitor voltage approaches the emf, less voltage is left across $R$
ch27.obs.switch: Switch to discharge halfway: discharge starts from the charge at that instant and the current reverses ($i < 0$)
ch27.obs.RC: Doubling $R$ or $C$ doubles $\tau$ and stretches the curves in time by 2. Changing $C$ while running keeps the charge $q$, so $V_C = q/C$ jumps
ch27.assume: Battery emf 12 V; internal and wire resistance neglected. A run that starts in discharge mode starts from a fully charged capacitor ($q = C\mathcal{E}$). Moving dots show the flow of positive charge (conventional current). The graphs span $10\tau$ (0.5–20 s); for $\tau < 0.5$ s time runs slower than real time (0.1× at $\tau = 0.05$ s)
ch27.assume.sym: $\mathcal{E}$: emf of the battery (12 V). $q$: charge on the upper (+) plate, $V_C = q/C$: voltage across the capacitor, $i$: current in the circuit (positive in the charging direction). $t_s$: time of the latest switch or $R$, $C$ change, $q_0$: the charge at that instant
ch27.assume.floor: Once less than one elementary charge $e$ = 1.60×10⁻¹⁹ C is left to flow, the exponential model has nothing left to describe (less than one electron): a discharged $q$ and $V_C$ print an exact 0, and the current prints as the bound $\lvert i\rvert < e/\tau$ rounded up to a power of ten ($< 10^{-14}$ mA at $\tau$ = 0.05 s)
ch27.assume.plate: A full row of ± symbols on a plate stands for the larger of $C\mathcal{E}$ and the largest charge of the run. Lowering $C$ while running keeps the charge, so $V_C$ rises above $\mathcal{E}$; the extra charge flows back toward the battery and the rows shrink
